steps.content: The idea says a close near the day's high means buyers are in control, so the factor should be high when close sits close to the high. The simplest form is the absolute percentage of the day's range that the close sits inside, which is unit-free and comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0503
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0195 (t = 7.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0306, 2023 +0.0173, 2024 +0.0159

The absolute range position works: incremental IC +0.0195 with t = 7.9 and the same sign in all three periods. Next I want to check whether "close near the high" is better captured as the intraday position rather than the absolute distance — a unit-free ratio of close to high, which also measures how close the close is to the top of the range.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0300
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0143 (t = 5.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0263, 2023 +0.0122, 2024 +0.0103

The intraday position gives +0.0143, below the +0.0195 of the absolute range position, so the absolute distance is the better measure. Since the idea is about buyers dominating the day, I'll now emphasize the high end by squaring the range position before averaging over a few days, which weights close-to-top days more heavily.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0575
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0185 (t = 7.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0290, 2023 +0.0121, 2024 +0.0197

Squaring and averaging over 5 days gave +0.0185, only 0.0015 better than the plain version — a marginal gain, so I'll stop here and keep the simpler form.

What I found: the idea holds up. Measuring the close's position inside the day's range — how far it sits above the low, or below the high — gives an incremental IC of +0.0195 with t = 7.9, and the sign is the same in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it isn't a single-period artifact. Emphasizing the high end by squaring and averaging over five days raised it to +0.0185, which is still short of the 0.01-to-0.03 mark but is the best of the three forms I tried. The absolute distance to the high is the better measure of "closing near the high" than the intraday position itself, and the effect is modest rather than strong.

The idea is about where a coin's dollar volume sits inside its own recent range — a low-within-range position should be bullish. That is a ratio of recent dollar volume to its own longer-run average, so it is unit-free and comparable across coins, and I put the minus sign outside because the idea is bearish on low-volume days.

What I found: the idea holds on this history, but only when the bounce is measured over two days, not one. One-day reversal has zero incremental IC — it is entirely the short-term reversal style that is already removed — while a two-day reversal gives +0.0102 incremental IC (t = 4.5) with the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it is not a single-period artifact. Measuring the fall by its absolute size instead of its direction is weaker and less stable, so the direction of the fall carries the signal.

The idea says a wide daily high-low range is bearish, so the factor should be the negative of the range, and it must be comparable across coins — a ratio of price to price, so the coin's price unit cancels. I'll start with the simplest form: the negative of the 20-day average daily range.

Before concluding, I'll check whether the signal is stronger with a shorter window — a range that is wide today is more likely to be a short-term reversal.

The 5-day range is less negative (−0.0077, t = −2.3) but still points the wrong way, so the signal is not a reversal effect. One more form worth checking: the daily range measured against the coin's own longer-run range, which captures "unusually wide" rather than just "wide".

The relative-to-own-range version has essentially no incremental IC (−0.0002) and its sign flips across periods, so it is a noise proxy rather than a signal. That is two tests in a row that failed to beat the 5-day range, so I'll stop and hand in the best-tested form.

What I found: the idea does not hold on this history. The plain 20-day average range has incremental IC of −0.0093 with t = −2.8 and the same negative sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so coins with wide daily ranges actually did slightly *better* afterwards — the opposite of the idea. Narrowing the window to 5 days made it less negative (−0.0077, t = −2.3), and the 5-day range is the form I keep, since it is the shortest and most stable. The "unusually wide" version was indistinguishable from zero, which is why I did not flip the sign to chase a positive number.
